evidence.evidenceSnippet: Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook are Google generative AI services available to all University of Michigan faculty, staff, and students. newClaim.claimText: U-M does not recommend the use of AI-detection technology given their high error rate. False positives and negatives are possible, and even likely.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Language models generalize and summarize existing knowledge based on probability predictions of word sequences rather than copying it verbatim, and so it may be impossible to identify their use with certainty. While detection tools like Turnitin or GPTZero may report probability of AI authorship, they are easily circumvented and cannot provide definitive proof of cheating. False positives and negatives are possible, and even likely. U-M does not recommend the use of AI-detection technology at this time given their high error rate.

Detection tools are imperfect, and currently no software is able to detect AI-generated text with 100% certainty. AI detection tools can be used to identify situations where further inquiry into the use of AI-generated text may be needed. They should not be considered a definitive measure for cheating.

newClaim.claimText: U-M guidance gives instructors flexibility to allow or disallow GenAI by course and assessment, with clear syllabus and assignment expectations; course policies should align with applicable school or college misconduct policies.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Instructors are disciplinary experts responsible for what is taught, appropriate pedagogies, and assessment methodologies. GenAI may influence all three, and as such, instructors need flexibility to allow or disallow the use of GenAI tools. If the latter policy is adopted, instructors should be aware that U-M does not currently support the use of surveillance and plagiarism detection tools as they cannot be reliably counted upon. Further, clear policies have to be formulated regarding punitive measures and how they may be enforced. If GenAI tools are allowed, the instructor should be clear which tools are allowed and in what capacity.

Teaching in the presence of ubiquitous GenAI tools should be considered a dynamic endeavor and necessitates flexibility. Approaches and expectations will vary by instructor, course, assessment, and activity. To ensure transparency, it is critical that expectations are clearly articulated in the syllabus and continually reinforced when assignments are given. Instructors should align their course policies with their college’s academic misconduct policies.

Specific uses of GenAI are encouraged (generating ideas, editing, translating, outlining)

Any use of GenAI constitutes academic misconduct.

newClaim.claimText: An LSA student found responsible may submit a written appeal to the Academic Judiciary Committee within two weeks from the date of the resolution letter, challenging responsibility, the college sanction or both. Grounds include serious procedural error, significant previously unavailable evidence or excessive college sanctions. Sanctions remain during appeal. Discrimination/prohibited-behavior claims must also go to ECRT and pause appeal. AJC may reverse responsibility or recommend keeping, reducing or increasing sanctions.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
A student who has been found responsible for academic misconduct may submit a written appeal to the LSA Academic Judiciary Committee (AJC), a committee composed of both undergraduate students and faculty members from the College of LSA.
Note: If students submit an appeal request, college- and course-level sanctions remain in place while it is pending. If an appeal is based on discrimination or other prohibited behavior, students must also file a report with the Equity, Civil Rights & Title IX Office (ECRT). The appeal process will pause until that matter is resolved.
Procedures
The student must submit an appeal within two weeks from the date of the resolution letter.
The appeal must state wh

at is being appealed: the finding of academic misconduct, the college sanction imposed, or both.
The appeal must also state and describe in detail at least one of the following grounds for appeal:
The procedure was violated in a way that seriously compromised the investigation and/or conclusions.
There is significant new evidence not reasonably available at the time of the meeting with the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee.
The college sanctions are excessive relative to the violation.
Appeals are not granted unless one or more of the above criteria are met and supported by evidence. 
Making a decision
A member of the AJC will decide whether the appeal has sufficient grounds to m

ove forward. If it does not, the appeal process ends and the Office of Student Academic Affairs' decision stands. There is no further appeal opportunity.
If it is determined that grounds for an appeal have been met, a panel of AJC members will review your case alongside evidence from the instructor and documentation of how the Office of Student Academic Affairs reached its decision.
After reviewing the appeal, the AJC may:
Reverse the finding of responsibility (overturn the original decision), or
Uphold the finding of responsibility. If it's upheld, the Committee may recommend that the Office of Student Affairs keep the sanction as is, reduce it, or increase it.
Students will be notified of
the outcome by email.

newClaim.claimText: In LSA SAA Resolution, the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee decides under the preponderance standard. Students receive allegations/evidence and may respond, present material and ask questions. Students should notify SAA when bringing a support person. The usual Honor Council participant does not advocate for or against the student.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
What an SAA Resolution is
A faculty or staff member within LSA who believes academic misconduct has occurred may file a formal complaint of academic misconduct with the LSA Office of Student Academic Affairs who will determine if misconduct has occurred.
Important: The instructor should not impose any penalty or require remedial work until the case has been resolved. Once a case has been filed with the Office of Student Academic Affairs, it may not be withdrawn without the approval of the Assistant Dean. Barring unforeseen circumstances, cases will be resolved within the academic term (and typically within three weeks) in which the incident occurs.
SAA Resolution Procedures
Reporting academi

c misconduct
Instructor reports a possible case of academic misconduct to SAA using the Report of Suspected Misconduct form
Prior to the Academic Misconduct Meeting
SAA sends an email to the student stating that an instructor has reported what they believe to be a possible case of academic misconduct. The email also includes a link to set up an Academic Misconduct Meeting. 
Once an appointment is scheduled, SAA sends a confirmation email which contains evidence about the allegations of misconduct. 
The Academic Misconduct Meeting will determine whether the student is responsible, or not, for the alleged misconduct. An accused student should prepare for the Academic Misconduct Meeting by revi

ewing the information provided, asking any clarifying questions, and show up ready to present any of their own relevant information, read any statement, and/or ask further questions. 
During the Academic Misconduct Meeting
The Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee will describe the allegations made, detail the supporting evidence, and review the range of college-level sanctions (e.g. disciplinary probation, suspension, or expulsion).
This is an opportunity for the student to be heard and to present their side of the incident. The student should be ready to present any relevant material, read a statement, and/or ask questions.
Typically, in each meeting a representative of the LSA Stu

dent Honor Council participates, though they do not advocate for or against the student.
Students should notify the Office of Student Academic Affairs if they will have a support person in attendance at the meeting.
In certain circumstances, the Coordinator of Academic Integrity may give the student the opportunity to ask questions of the accusing party, either by exchanging written questions or by asking questions during a subsequent meeting. This additional step will be completed prior to the Coordinator or designee’s final decision.
The meeting between the accused student and the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee may be virtual or in-person.
Making a decision
The Coordinator o

f Academic Integrity or designee determines whether a violation of the LSA Community Expectations of Academic Integrity has occurred and if the student is responsible for academic misconduct.
The standard of review is preponderance. This means that the student is not considered responsible unless the evidence demonstrates that it is "more likely than not" that academic misconduct has occurred.
The student will be informed by letter, with an email copy to the instructor(s), of the decision and sanction(s), if any, to be imposed.
If a student is found not responsible for academic misconduct, the instructor(s) will grade the student accordingly.

newClaim.claimText: In LSA, course-grade penalties follow the instructor’s syllabus/department policies; SAA may assign college sanctions including probation, reflective essay, suspension or expulsion. These are possible outcomes, not an automatic AI penalty.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:

Course-level sanctions: appropriate grade penalties for the misconduct will be left up to the instructor based on syllabus grade policies or department policies, if applicable.
College-level sanctions: The student may be assigned college sanctions by the Office of Student Academic Affairs. Examples of these sanctions include: 
Disciplinary probation - students are placed on probation for one year. As part of this process, a notation is placed on the student's unofficial transcript. This notation serves as a warning and reprimand that the student has been found responsible for academic misconduct. After that one year period, the notat

ion is removed provided no further violations of academic misconduct have occurred.
Reflective Essay - the student must write an essay about their experience, share what they have learned from it, and discuss how they intend to incorporate LSA Community Expectations into their personal and academic life moving forward.
Suspension - the student is ineligible to enroll at the university for one semester and a permanent notation is added to their transcript. In order to re-enroll in future terms, the student must write a petition for reactivation at least two weeks prior to the start of the term they wish to enroll.
Expulsion - The student is permanently removed from the university.

newClaim.claimText: LSA instructors may use Instructor Resolution for non-egregious incidents meriting no consequence greater than zero on the assignment; remedial work may also apply. SAA Resolution is appropriate for possible course failure or more severe sanctions, previous responsibility findings, or falsified academic documents. While pending, students are presumed not responsible, may attend class, cannot drop/change grading option, and instructors may not impose penalties/remedial work. A pending end-of-term case may receive NR and prevents course credit/graduation.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
An instructor within LSA who believes academic misconduct has occurred may choose either
Instructor Resolution: Resolve the matter directly with the student
Appropriate when: the incident is not egregious and merits no consequence greater than a zero on the assignment, though the student may be required to do additional, remedial work (e.g., rewrite a paper).
SAA Resolution: File a complaint to the Office of Student Academic Affairs, who will resolve the case. 
Appropriate when: the sanction may result in the student failing the course or more severe sanction, the student has a previous finding of responsibility, or the student is suspected of falsifying or misrepresenting academic documents

.
 
Examples of academic misconduct include, but are not limited to: cheating, plagiarism, inappropriate collaboration, falsification of data, records, or documents, and aiding and abetting dishonesty.
Deadlines: The complaint for any alleged instance of academic misconduct should be filed as soon as practical from the date of occurrence and should be submitted within 2 months of the date of the incident.
Privacy: Materials related to a formal complaint of academic misconduct or an instructor's report of a resolution will be maintained by the Office of Student Academic Affairs in compliance with the privacy expectations under the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA).
While a mis

conduct case is pending, with either Instruction Resolution or SAA Resolution:
The student is presumed to not be responsible for the alleged misconduct and the student may continue to attend class and receive grades.
The instructor may NOT impose any penalty or require any remedial work until the case has been resolved.
The student may NOT change registration in the course (e.g. drop the course or change the grading option to Pass/Fail).
If the term ends and a final grade must be reported while a case is pending, the instructor should use the grade NR (No Report). NR is a temporary, neutral grade that may be used in special circumstances where a final grade is not yet able to be reported. Th

newClaim.claimText: U-M sample syllabi allow instructors to specify GenAI disclosure, restrictions, or bans by activity, in alignment with college policy; examples are not automatically binding campus-wide rules.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
Teaching in the presence of ubiquitous GenAI tools should be considered a dynamic endeavor and necessitates flexibility. Approaches and expectations will vary by instructor, course, assessment, and activity. To ensure transparency, it is critical that expectations are clearly articulated in the syllabus and continually reinforced when assignments are given. Instructors should align their course policies with their college’s academic misconduct policies.
Instructors are disciplinary experts responsible for what is taught, appropriate pedagogies, and assessment methodologies. GenAI may influence all three, and as such, instructors need flexibility to allow or disallow the use of GenAI tools. I

f the latter policy is adopted, instructors should be aware that U-M does not currently support the use of surveillance and plagiarism detection tools as they cannot be reliably counted upon. Further, clear policies have to be formulated regarding punitive measures and how they may be enforced. If GenAI tools are allowed, the instructor should be clear which tools are allowed and in what capacity.
It is also important to point out to students that although AI-generated content may appear reliable and factual, that is not always the case, and that inaccuracies, untruths, and false citations may be missed if one is overly reliant on the tools.
Syllabus Language
GenAI is changing rapidly, and n

ew tools will become available. Course policies therefore need to be provisional and subject to change. Several principles can guide instructors to develop course policies appropriate for their contexts:
Protect cognitive dimension of learning: GenAI should enhance, not hinder, learning.
Responsibility for content: Students are responsible for all content (ideas, facts, citations), however the work is generated. (Note: Chat GPT can generate untrue, biased, inaccurate, and hallucinatory content.)
Require ethical transparency: Students should be transparent about how they use GenAI and adhere to standards of academic integrity.
Explain academic misconduct: Instructors should distinguish betwee

n allowed and disallowed uses of GenAI, including how, when, and why GenAI may (not) be used.
Course policies might fall into one of three categories:
Specific uses of GenAI are encouraged (generating ideas, editing, translating, outlining)
Specific uses of GenAI are allowed if students clearly distinguish between their original work and GenAI output (highlighting output, tracking changes in GenAI output)
Any use of GenAI constitutes academic misconduct.

Google Gemini is offered through U-M Google services for eligible faculty, staff, and students; sponsored affiliates, alumni, and retirees are excluded. Service use is subject to ITS terms and per-service data restrictions, not universal assignment permission.

U-M GPT is an ITS-provided conversational AI service for active U-M users. Access is governed by ITS terms, including U.S.-only use and data safeguards; availability does not authorize all academic assessments.
U-M GPT Toolkit is an ITS-provided advanced generative AI service with access through its self-service API gateway. Use remains subject to U-M terms, data permissions, and course rules.

U-M Maizey is an ITS-provided generative AI service allowing authorized U-M users to work with custom datasets, subject to service terms and data classification rules; access does not imply assignment permission.
U-M does not recommend the use of AI-detection technology given their high error rate. False positives and negatives are possible, and even likely.

U-M directs community members to approved AI services for institutional data. Services without a U-M contract or data agreement should only receive Low-classified institutional data. U-M Google guidance allows certain sensitive categories only as detailed in the service guide; the authenticated matrix remains unavailable.

U-M guidance calls for human review of AI-generated code and professionally trained peer code reviews for all new or significantly changed applications, particularly those handling Restricted or High data.

ITS states that its AI Services include HIPAA safeguards and may be used with PHI, and explicitly directs users to the service-specific Sensitive Data Guide for permitted types. The authenticated guide was not revalidated; this is not blanket PHI authorization.
U-M requires AI use in teaching and learning to align with principles of honesty, candor, openness, and integrity in scholarship and research, including appropriate disclosure and citation.

U-M guidance gives instructors flexibility to allow or disallow GenAI by course and assessment, with clear syllabus and assignment expectations; course policies should align with applicable school or college misconduct policies.

U-M cautions students that, in most cases, data entered into external GenAI tools are not private and may be accessible to their providers, and advises against sharing private or sensitive information.
ITS AI service and Google services have a U.S.-only usage condition under U-M terms (May 2025).

U-M ITS AI data are not used for model training, but service input, prompt history, usage metadata and logs are processed, including sharing prompt data with cloud vendors. The notice does not establish a uniform retention period.
U-M Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) exclude sponsored affiliates, alumni and retirees; supported sensitive data vary by approved guide.
OVPR internal peer-review guidance updated August 11, 2025 discourages generative AI reviewing and strongly discourages uploading other researchers’ grant proposals to commercial AI tools.
The School of Nursing faculty guide advises that AI should not be the sole basis for grading and restricts uploads of identifiable student work unless the service and use are approved.

ITS does not provide a campus-wide teaching/learning plagiarism checking system. Detector output can trigger inquiry but is not definitive proof, while iThenticate is described for researchers’ own work, not student evaluation.
Procurement Services should be the sole purchaser for AI services intended for institutional Moderate, High, or Restricted data; access alone does not confer approval for each sensitive data type.
U-M sample syllabi allow instructors to specify GenAI disclosure, restrictions, or bans by activity, in alignment with college policy; examples are not automatically binding campus-wide rules.

LSA instructors may use Instructor Resolution for non-egregious incidents meriting no consequence greater than zero on the assignment; remedial work may also apply. SAA Resolution is appropriate for possible course failure or more severe sanctions, previous responsibility findings, or falsified academic documents. While pending, students are presumed not responsible, may attend class, cannot drop/change grading option, and instructors may not impose penalties/remedial work. A pending end-of-term case may receive NR and prevents course credit/graduation.

In LSA SAA Resolution, the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee decides under the preponderance standard. Students receive allegations/evidence and may respond, present material and ask questions. Students should notify SAA when bringing a support person. The usual Honor Council participant does not advocate for or against the student.

In LSA, course-grade penalties follow the instructor’s syllabus/department policies; SAA may assign college sanctions including probation, reflective essay, suspension or expulsion. These are possible outcomes, not an automatic AI penalty.

An LSA student found responsible may submit a written appeal to the Academic Judiciary Committee within two weeks from the date of the resolution letter, challenging responsibility, the college sanction or both. Grounds include serious procedural error, significant previously unavailable evidence or excessive college sanctions. Sanctions remain during appeal. Discrimination/prohibited-behavior claims must also go to ECRT and pause appeal. AJC may reverse responsibility or recommend keeping, reducing or increasing sanctions.

For another school’s student in an LSA course, SAA determines the course integrity violation and instructor course sanction authority; the student’s home school imposes college sanctions, including any recommendations it accepts.

claimChanges.claimText: U-M ITS offers a generative AI platform to active faculty, staff, and students across its campuses and Michigan Medicine, subject to the ITS AI Services terms that limit use to within the United States.

Adobe Firefly is available through U-M enterprise Adobe licensing to eligible faculty, staff, and students at no added individual cost. This institutional availability is not blanket permission for coursework, examinations, or sensitive-data uploads.

Google Gemini is offered through U-M Google services for eligible faculty, staff, and students; sponsored affiliates, alumni, and retirees are excluded. Service use is subject to ITS terms and per-service data restrictions, not universal assignment permission.

U-M GPT is an ITS-provided conversational AI service for active U-M users. Access is governed by ITS terms, including U.S.-only use and data safeguards; availability does not authorize all academic assessments.
U-M GPT Toolkit is an ITS-provided advanced generative AI service with access through its self-service API gateway. Use remains subject to U-M terms, data permissions, and course rules.

U-M Maizey is an ITS-provided generative AI service allowing authorized U-M users to work with custom datasets, subject to service terms and data classification rules; access does not imply assignment permission.
U-M does not recommend the use of AI-detection technology given their high error rate. False positives and negatives are possible, and even likely.

U-M directs community members to approved AI services for institutional data. Services without a U-M contract or data agreement should only receive Low-classified institutional data. U-M Google guidance allows certain sensitive categories only as detailed in the service guide; the authenticated matrix remains unavailable.

U-M guidance calls for human review of AI-generated code and professionally trained peer code reviews for all new or significantly changed applications, particularly those handling Restricted or High data.

ITS states that its AI Services include HIPAA safeguards and may be used with PHI, and explicitly directs users to the service-specific Sensitive Data Guide for permitted types. The authenticated guide was not revalidated; this is not blanket PHI authorization.
U-M requires AI use in teaching and learning to align with principles of honesty, candor, openness, and integrity in scholarship and research, including appropriate disclosure and citation.

U-M guidance gives instructors flexibility to allow or disallow GenAI by course and assessment, with clear syllabus and assignment expectations; course policies should align with applicable school or college misconduct policies.

U-M cautions students that, in most cases, data entered into external GenAI tools are not private and may be accessible to their providers, and advises against sharing private or sensitive information.
ITS AI service and Google services have a U.S.-only usage condition under U-M terms (May 2025).

U-M ITS AI data are not used for model training, but service input, prompt history, usage metadata and logs are processed, including sharing prompt data with cloud vendors. The notice does not establish a uniform retention period.
U-M Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) exclude sponsored affiliates, alumni and retirees; supported sensitive data vary by approved guide.
OVPR internal peer-review guidance updated August 11, 2025 discourages generative AI reviewing and strongly discourages uploading other researchers’ grant proposals to commercial AI tools.
The School of Nursing faculty guide advises that AI should not be the sole basis for grading and restricts uploads of identifiable student work unless the service and use are approved.

ITS does not provide a campus-wide teaching/learning plagiarism checking system. Detector output can trigger inquiry but is not definitive proof, while iThenticate is described for researchers’ own work, not student evaluation.
Procurement Services should be the sole purchaser for AI services intended for institutional Moderate, High, or Restricted data; access alone does not confer approval for each sensitive data type.
U-M sample syllabi allow instructors to specify GenAI disclosure, restrictions, or bans by activity, in alignment with college policy; examples are not automatically binding campus-wide rules.

LSA instructors may use Instructor Resolution for non-egregious incidents meriting no consequence greater than zero on the assignment; remedial work may also apply. SAA Resolution is appropriate for possible course failure or more severe sanctions, previous responsibility findings, or falsified academic documents. While pending, students are presumed not responsible, may attend class, cannot drop/change grading option, and instructors may not impose penalties/remedial work. A pending end-of-term case may receive NR and prevents course credit/graduation.

In LSA SAA Resolution, the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee decides under the preponderance standard. Students receive allegations/evidence and may respond, present material and ask questions. Students should notify SAA when bringing a support person. The usual Honor Council participant does not advocate for or against the student.

In LSA, course-grade penalties follow the instructor’s syllabus/department policies; SAA may assign college sanctions including probation, reflective essay, suspension or expulsion. These are possible outcomes, not an automatic AI penalty.

An LSA student found responsible may submit a written appeal to the Academic Judiciary Committee within two weeks from the date of the resolution letter, challenging responsibility, the college sanction or both. Grounds include serious procedural error, significant previously unavailable evidence or excessive college sanctions. Sanctions remain during appeal. Discrimination/prohibited-behavior claims must also go to ECRT and pause appeal. AJC may reverse responsibility or recommend keeping, reducing or increasing sanctions.

For another school’s student in an LSA course, SAA determines the course integrity violation and instructor course sanction authority; the student’s home school imposes college sanctions, including any recommendations it accepts.

LSA instructors may use Instructor Resolution for non-egregious incidents meriting no consequence greater than zero on the assignment; remedial work may also apply. SAA Resolution is appropriate for possible course failure or more severe sanctions, previous responsibility findings, or falsified academic documents. While pending, students are presumed not responsible, may attend class, cannot drop/change grading option, and instructors may not impose penalties/remedial work. A pending end-of-term case may receive NR and prevents course credit/graduation.

In LSA SAA Resolution, the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee decides under the preponderance standard. Students receive allegations/evidence and may respond, present material and ask questions. Students should notify SAA when bringing a support person. The usual Honor Council participant does not advocate for or against the student.

In LSA, course-grade penalties follow the instructor’s syllabus/department policies; SAA may assign college sanctions including probation, reflective essay, suspension or expulsion. These are possible outcomes, not an automatic AI penalty.

An LSA student found responsible may submit a written appeal to the Academic Judiciary Committee within two weeks from the date of the resolution letter, challenging responsibility, the college sanction or both. Grounds include serious procedural error, significant previously unavailable evidence or excessive college sanctions. Sanctions remain during appeal. Discrimination/prohibited-behavior claims must also go to ECRT and pause appeal. AJC may reverse responsibility or recommend keeping, reducing or increasing sanctions.

For another school’s student in an LSA course, SAA determines the course integrity violation and instructor course sanction authority; the student’s home school imposes college sanctions, including any recommendations it accepts.
